crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: AI and authorship concerns who or what counts as an author when AI systems help produce text, images, code, data, or research outputs. It covers academic papers, books, reports, journalism, creative works, and software, and it asks how credit, responsibility, and accountability are assigned. In research integrity, the focus is on disclosure of AI use, verification of claims, and the difference between assistance and substantive contribution. The topic also touches copyright, plagiarism, peer review, and the evidentiary record that shows how a work was made.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Authorship questions run on the systems that produce and track scholarly and creative work. These include word processors, reference managers, preprint servers, journal submission systems, repositories, and AI writing or coding assistants. Provenance infrastructure matters, such as version control, audit logs, metadata standards, and persistent identifiers for people, works, and datasets. The site's library indexes 12646 claims extracted from research works, which shows how a claim can be traced to its original paper.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Researchers and integrity officers examine authorship statements, contributor role taxonomies, disclosure forms, and publication policies. They compare drafts, prompts, model outputs, and edits where records exist, and they check whether claims in a paper are supported by the cited evidence. Bibliometric and text analysis can detect patterns, but human judgment is needed to distinguish assistance from authorship. The method also includes interviews, correspondence with authors, and review of institutional guidelines.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: AI use raises questions about copyright ownership, license terms, confidentiality, and the potential for fabricated references or unsupported claims. Provenance is central, because a clear record of which model, version, prompt, and data were used helps others assess reliability and reproduce results. Institutions and publishers often have policies on disclosure, but these vary, and the legal status of AI generated content differs by jurisdiction. The site's practice of linking to original papers, not to the Consensus search tool, reflects a broader commitment to traceable sources. Risks include attribution errors, plagiarism, bias, and the erosion of accountability if no human can answer for the work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more granular contribution statements, machine readable provenance, and tools that log AI interactions as part of the research record. Journals, funders, and institutions are likely to refine policies as courts and regulators address copyright and liability. Authorship may shift from a binary label to a layered record of human and machine contributions. The growing catalogue of scientific models, AI tools, and glossary terms suggests that terminology and tooling will keep changing, so governance will need to keep pace. Education and peer review will also adapt to ask what a human author actually did.
